patient.chief_complaint: Progressive gait and cognitive decline labeled as PSP — second opinion requested because patient has not fallen from postural instability alone and tap trial was not offered
patient.history_present_illness: A 74-year-old retired mechanic was referred by his family for a second opinion. He was given a working diagnosis of progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) by a community neurologist 18 months ago, based on his gait deterioration, cognitive decline, and mildly reduced upward gaze. Since that diagnosis, no LP or tap trial has been offered, and he has continued to deteriorate. His son, who has done research on PSP and NPH, is requesting a formal workup including LP and possibly tap trial. The patient's wife notes his walking difficulties began approximately 2.5 years ago — she describes a shuffling wide-based gait with freezing at doorways, not the classic backward falls of PSP. He has had four falls — all forward, one to the side, none from pure backward postural instability. Urinary urgency and incontinence began approximately 18 months ago. His cognitive decline over the same period includes worsening forgetfulness and executive dysfunction. The community neurologist diagnosed PSP based on: mildly slow vertical saccades (though not absent), prominent falls, and gait disorder. A head MRI was reported as showing 'possible midbrain atrophy.' However, the family notes that re-review of the MRI at the academic center shows Evans index 0.36 — not mentioned in the community read. The key diagnostic challenge is distinguishing NPH from PSP, or determining whether NPH is superimposed on a PSP-spectrum disorder.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented x3. MoCA 22/30. Mild delayed recall (2/5), executive dysfunction. Mildly reduced facial expression. No aphasia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: PERRL. Vertical gaze: mild slowing of upward saccades — velocity reduced. Downward saccades normal velocity. NO complete vertical gaze palsy. Horizontal gaze normal. Smooth pursuit mildly saccadic. No square-wave jerks.
neurological_exam.motor: Mild symmetric axial rigidity (neck, trunk). No resting tremor. No appendicular rigidity. No cogwheel rigidity.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, magnetic shuffling gait. Freezing prominent. Steps very short. TUG 34 seconds. Falls: forward and sideways — NOT predominantly backward from postural instability. Cannot tandem walk. Pull test — 2 steps backward (not extreme retropulsion).
neurological_exam.additional: Mild axial rigidity. No upper motor neuron signs. Bilateral grasp reflexes. No nuchal rigidity. Mild hypomimia.

signal_characteristics.description: Evans index 0.36 — missed on prior community read
Tight high-convexity sulci with enlarged Sylvian fissures

mri.impression: Evans index 0.36 (unreported on prior community read), callosal angle 80°, DESH pattern, prominent aqueductal flow void. Midbrain-pons area ratio 0.55 — above PSP threshold. No confirmed midbrain atrophy. Prior 'possible midbrain atrophy' appears to have been overstated. Clinical correlation recommended.

specialized_test.test_type: High-volume tap trial (40 mL) — FIRST tap trial in 2.5 years of symptoms
specialized_test.impression: Clearly positive tap trial — 32% TUG improvement, 35% walk improvement, 3-point MoCA improvement at 24 hours. The working PSP diagnosis appears to be incorrect. This is NPH, not PSP. VP shunt is urgently indicated — this patient has been delayed 2.5 years. Excellent prognosis given positive tap trial and lack of confirmed PSP features.
recommended_actions: Urgent VP shunt referral — significant diagnostic delay must be addressed
Reassess PSP diagnosis — formally exclude with neuro-ophthalmology
Family communication: working diagnosis revision from PSP to iNPH

findings.finding: Upward saccades: velocity mildly reduced (60% of normal) but NOT absent. Downward saccades: normal velocity and accuracy. No square-wave jerks. Convergence normal. No oculomotor palsy.
Pattern: mild slowing of upward voluntary saccades. Does NOT meet MDS PSP diagnostic criteria (requires vertical supranuclear gaze palsy affecting downward saccades or complete vertical gaze palsy).

output.impression: Mild upward saccade slowing only — does NOT meet PSP diagnostic criteria. PSP requires downward gaze palsy or complete vertical gaze palsy; this patient has only mildly slow upward saccades. This level of oculomotor dysfunction is within the differential for NPH with frontal lobe dysfunction. PSP diagnosis is NOT supported. iNPH is the correct diagnosis.
recommended_actions: Revise working diagnosis from PSP to iNPH
Proceed with VP shunt referral urgently

findings.result: Normal bilateral striatal dopamine transporter uptake. No putaminal or caudate loss. Normal symmetric pattern.

output.impression: Normal DaTscan — no nigrostriatal degeneration. Parkinson's disease and DLB excluded. PSP typically shows reduced striatal uptake — absence of this finding further argues against PSP. Consistent with iNPH.

output.modality: Formal MRI midbrain volumetry and MPAR calculation
output.impression: MPAR 0.55 — above PSP threshold of 0.52. No hummingbird sign, no morning glory sign. Formal volumetry does NOT support PSP. Prior community report of 'possible midbrain atrophy' was inaccurate on formal measurement. MRI is consistent with NPH, not PSP.
Negative amyloid PET. No Alzheimer's copathology. Confirmed iNPH — excellent VP shunt prognosis.

results.title: NPH misdiagnosed as PSP — case series and distinguishing features
results.key_finding: NPH may be misdiagnosed as PSP due to overlapping gait features; key distinguishing features: (1) NPH: wide-based magnetic, forward falls, Evans index >0.3; (2) PSP: narrow-based, predominant backward falls, complete downward gaze palsy, MPAR <0.52; tap trial is diagnostic

results.title: Tap trial in suspected PSP — identifying NPH superimposition
results.key_finding: Tap trial should be performed in all patients with ventriculomegaly regardless of PSP concern; positive tap trial identifies NPH component and is a treatable finding

output.summary: Key PSP-NPH distinguishing features: (1) Falls: NPH tends forward/sideways; PSP characteristically backward; (2) Gait: NPH wide-based magnetic; PSP narrow-based upright; (3) Ocular: PSP requires downward gaze palsy; NPH has no mandatory oculomotor signs; (4) MPAR: NPH >0.52; PSP <0.52; (5) DaTscan: NPH normal; PSP often reduced. This patient's features consistently support NPH, not PSP.

differential.key_features: No complete vertical gaze palsy, no downward gaze palsy; MPAR 0.55 (above PSP threshold); normal DaTscan; no hummingbird sign; falls forward not backward. PSP diagnosis criteria not met.
Normal DaTscan. No typical PD features (narrow-based festinant gait, resting tremor, asymmetric cogwheel rigidity).
Mild white matter changes and hypertension; however Evans 0.36 and clearly positive tap trial confirm NPH as dominant process
Normal CSF biomarkers, negative amyloid PET (CL 11)

critical_actions: Formal MPAR measurement — subjective 'possible midbrain atrophy' on community read was incorrect
Formal video oculomotor exam — mild upward saccade slowing does NOT meet PSP criteria
Tap trial must be offered — should have been done 2.5 years ago when symptoms first appeared
Communicate diagnostic revision clearly to patient, family, and referring neurologist
contraindicated_actions: Accepting prior PSP diagnosis without verification — midbrain volumetry was informal and incorrect
Deferring tap trial because of PSP label — tap trial should be offered in any patient with ventriculomegaly
Starting levodopa empirically for presumed PSP without tap trial — this is NPH
key_reasoning_points: PSP requires downward gaze palsy or complete vertical gaze palsy — mild upward saccade slowing alone is insufficient
MPAR 0.55 is above PSP threshold (0.52) — prior 'possible midbrain atrophy' was informal and incorrect
Normal DaTscan and wide-based magnetic gait (not narrow festinant) both argue against PSP
Falls were forward/sideways — PSP classically produces backward falls from truncal rigidity and retropulsion
Evans 0.36 was missed on community MRI read — formal re-read is essential in suspected movement disorders with gait change
Clearly positive tap trial (32%) definitively establishes NPH and refutes PSP as primary diagnosis

red_herrings.data_point: Working diagnosis of PSP from community neurologist based on mildly slow vertical saccades and gait disorder
red_herrings.intended_effect: PSP label prevents LP and tap trial from being offered; patient deteriorates without treatable NPH diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild upward saccade slowing does NOT meet PSP criteria; MPAR 0.55 is above PSP threshold; Evans 0.36 was missed. Formal evaluation reveals iNPH, not PSP.

red_herrings.data_point: 'Possible midbrain atrophy' on community MRI read

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Formal MPAR calculation (0.55) shows midbrain atrophy is NOT present by standard criteria. DESH, Evans 0.36, and callosal angle 80° were not reported by the community radiologist.
